blocks.text:
The quantities this bucket works with.
a: Coefficient of the unknown in the worked equation (3 dimensionless)
b: Constant added on the left of the worked equation (2 dimensionless)
c: Value the left side must equal in the worked equation (9 dimensionless)
x: The solution of the worked equation, recorded exactly (7/3 dimensionless)
x~: A twelve-digit truncation of the solution, which is a different number (2.333333333333 dimensionless)

blocks.meaning: Subtracting b and dividing by a non-zero a isolates the unknown using reversible operations, so the solution set is unchanged.
symbols: a: Coefficient of the unknown; must not be zero
b: Constant added on the left
c: Value the left side must equal
conditions: a is non-zero; if a = 0 the statement is either never true or always true.
Both operations are reversible, which is why the solution set is preserved.
The declared domain is the rationals.

correspondence.element: Marked solution with its exact label
correspondence.in_words: the one point on the line where substituting gives 9 and nothing is left over
the whole numbers either side, which the truncated decimal sits between without landing on the marked point

scene.frame: The rationals, drawn on a single axis with integer ticks.
scene.caption: x = 7/3 is the solution; 2.333333333333 is a different point, closed on the line but open as a solution because substituting it gives 8.999999999999, not 9.

blocks.text:
Where the hard work is.
An equation constrains an unknown. (MEDIUM) Learners arriving from arithmetic read the equals sign as an instruction to compute, and that reading survives unless it is confronted directly.
Operations that preserve the solution set. (MEDIUM) The steps are memorable as a procedure, which is exactly why the reversibility condition behind them goes unnoticed until it fails.
An exact solution is not its decimal approximation. (MEDIUM) Calculator habits teach that a decimal is the finished answer, so a fraction reads as unfinished work rather than as the exact value.
